items.title: COVID exposed how thin most supply chains were
items.claim: During 2020-22, automotive production was held back by shortages of one component category in particular. Which was it?

options.text: Semiconductors (chips) — the global shortage cost the automotive industry an estimated $210 billion in lost revenue in 2021 alone (AlixPartners)

items.reveal:
When auto demand fell in spring 2020, car makers cancelled chip orders. Foundries (TSMC, Samsung) reallocated capacity to consumer electronics, where demand was surging. When car demand returned, chip capacity was booked out. Ford alone lost around 1.25 million units of production in 2021.

The US CHIPS Act (2022) and EU Chips Act (2023) responded with $50bn+ in subsidies for domestic semiconductor manufacturing — a direct strategic response to the disruption.
items.why: Multi-tier supply chains hide concentration risk. A car maker can have hundreds of direct suppliers but still depend on two or three foundries for chips.

items.title: Blockbuster could have bought Netflix for $50 million in 2000
items.claim: In 2000, Netflix was a struggling DVD-by-mail service. What did Blockbuster's CEO John Antioco do when Reed Hastings flew to Dallas to propose a sale?

options.text: Agreed in principle but the deal collapsed over terms
Laughed Hastings out of the room
Counter-offered to buy Netflix for $200 million
Bought a minority stake to monitor the technology

items.reveal_title: The room where it didn't happen
items.reveal:
Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph have both told the story (Randolph's book 'That Will Never Work' has the most colour). They proposed Blockbuster acquire Netflix for $50 million and run blockbuster.com as the online arm. Antioco — facing a profitable late-fee business model — declined.

Blockbuster did later launch an online service (Blockbuster Online) and was on a recovery path under Antioco, but a 2005 boardroom fight with activist investor Carl Icahn led to Antioco's departure and the strategy's reversal. Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010.

Netflix's market cap is now over $300 billion.
items.why: Disruption isn't usually about technology incumbents can't access; it's about business models they can't bring themselves to attack. Late fees were too profitable to risk.

items.title: Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975
items.claim: Steven Sasson, a Kodak engineer, built the first digital camera prototype in 1975. What happened to it?

options.text: Kodak rushed it to market and dominated the digital camera industry
Kodak management, worried about cannibalising film sales, suppressed the project; the company filed for bankruptcy in 2012 having failed the digital transition
It was stolen by a competitor before it could be developed

items.reveal:
Sasson's prototype was a 3.6 kg device using a CCD sensor and a cassette tape, taking 23 seconds to capture a 0.01 megapixel black-and-white image. He filed a patent in 1978.

Kodak's response, as Sasson later recalled, was 'that's cute, but don't tell anyone about it.' Film and processing had 60-70% gross margins. Kodak did launch digital products from the 1990s but couldn't restructure around a business model with lower margins.

The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2012.
items.why: Owning the future technology isn't enough — you have to be willing to destroy your current revenue. Few large organisations can.
